introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

La règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées sans source consultable. Les exemples cites sont des exemples reconnus ; aucune statistique precise n'est avancee. Les faits cites sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Question 6(c) : « For each case » désigne les deux problèmes cités (embouteillages, évacuation des déchets) : deux mesures chacun, soit quatre. Le recours à une entreprise spécialisée pour la collecte des déchets dans les grandes villes camerounaises est mentionné sans nom ni date. À faire vérifier.
Question 6(b) : le sujet imprime « sub-urbanization » avec un trait d'union, recopié tel quel.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Discuss THREE factors which influence the site of early rural settlements.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **site** of a settlement is the actual piece of land on which it is built. The early rural settlements (villages and hamlets) were located where people could find the basic needs for survival and protection. Three main factors are the following.

1. **Water supply.** Water for drinking, cooking, washing, livestock and farming was the first need, so that early villages were built beside springs, rivers, lakes and wells (**wet-point sites**), as along the valleys and spring lines of many regions. Settlements on permeable rock (chalk and limestone) are found at the springs at the foot of the scarp. Rivers also provide fish and transport.
2. **Dry-point sites and relief.** Where the land was marshy or liable to flooding, settlers chose slightly higher, dry and well-drained ground (**dry points**: river terraces, levees, low hills and islands in the swamps) which was free from flooding, damp and disease (such as malaria). Gentle slopes with a southerly or sunny aspect gave warmth and shelter from the wind. Flat and fertile land near the settlement allowed the cultivation of crops.
3. **Defence.** In times of insecurity, wars and slave raids, the early settlers chose **defensive sites**: hilltops, rock outcrops, river bends and meanders (which give protection on three sides), islands and caves, which could be easily defended (the hill-top villages of the Mandara mountains and of the Grassfields chiefdoms of Cameroon, and of the Mediterranean region).

Other factors include **fertile soil and nearness to farmland** (alluvial soils), **building materials** (wood, stone, clay), **fuel** from the forest and the **availability of grazing land and routes** or crossing points for trade. Religious and political reasons (the location of a chief's palace or a shrine) were also important. **Conclusion:** the site was chosen to supply water, a safe and dry place for the buildings, and defence, with the farmland and materials nearby.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Examine TWO reasons responsible for the increasing rate of sub-urbanization in the developed countries.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Sub-urbanization** is the growth of the suburbs, the residential and commercial areas on the edge of the cities (the outward movement of people, jobs and services from the inner city to the periphery). Two reasons for its increasing rate in developed countries are the following.

1. **Improved transport and rising car ownership.** The growth of car ownership, the construction of motorways and ring roads and the extension of commuter rail and bus services (and the cheapness of fuel and transport relative to income) allow people to live far from their workplaces and to commute daily. Telecommunications and home working also reduce the need to live near the workplace.
2. **Push factors in the inner city and pull factors of the suburbs.** The **push factors** include congestion, noise, air pollution, crime, ageing and crowded housing and high land prices in the city centre; the **pull factors** are cheaper and larger houses with gardens, cleaner air, more green space, better schools and a safer environment, which are made possible by rising incomes and by the availability of mortgages (housing loans). Planning policies that provide new housing estates and the movement of industry, offices, shopping centres and business parks to the edge of the town (decentralisation) also bring jobs and services close to the suburbs.

**Conclusion:** the combination of mobility, higher incomes and the search for a better environment, together with decentralised jobs and shops, explains the continued growth of the suburbs in developed countries.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) For each case, discuss TWO measures of redressing the problems of traffic congestion and waste disposal.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The question asks for two measures for **each** problem, that is, four measures in all, in towns such as Douala, Yaounde, Lagos or London.

**A. Traffic congestion** (slow movement of vehicles, delays, accidents, air pollution and noise caused by too many vehicles on roads that are too few and too narrow).

1. **Improve and promote public transport** (buses, bus rapid transit lanes, trams, metros and commuter trains; reliable, cheap and comfortable services) so that people leave their cars at home. Examples are the metro systems of London and Paris and the bus rapid transit lines built in cities such as Lagos.
2. **Manage the use of private cars and the road space.** Congestion charges and road pricing (London, Singapore), higher parking charges and parking restrictions, car-pooling, one-way streets and ring roads that keep the through traffic out of the centre, staggered working hours, and the widening and proper maintenance of the roads and junctions together with traffic lights and traffic police.

**B. Waste disposal** (the uncollected rubbish, blocked drains, bad smell, disease and pollution caused by the large quantity of solid waste produced by the town).

1. **Improve the collection and the safe disposal of waste.** Provide enough bins and collection vehicles, organise regular collection (by the municipality, or by a specialised company, as in the contracts for waste collection in the main Cameroonian cities), and replace open dumps by **sanitary landfills** or by **incineration** with energy recovery, in places away from houses and water sources.
2. **Reduce, re-use and recycle.** Encourage the sorting of waste at home, the recycling of paper, glass, metal and plastic, **composting** of organic waste, and the reduction of packaging, supported by public education campaigns, by fines for illegal dumping and by the involvement of the communities and small enterprises in the collection and the recycling.

**Conclusion:** both problems are made worse by rapid urban growth, and the measures work best when planning, investment, law enforcement and public cooperation are combined.
